Sharar

Fast agentic inference on unified-memory devices

Yahya Emara1* · Chi-Chih Chang1* · Anthony Fei1 · Ahmed F. AbouElhamayed1 · Chong-Yan Chen2 · Hung-Yueh Chiang3 · Kai-Chiang Wu4 · Mohamed S. Abdelfattah1

Paper · coming soon Code · coming soon Explore the techniques ↓

On a single DGX Spark serving Qwen and Nemotron models of up to 125B parameters, Sharar completes up to 3.1× more agentic tasks per hour and delivers up to 4.3× higher decoding throughput than vLLM, llama.cpp, and TensorFold.

103 tok/s
Single-user decode, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, SPEED-Bench 16k. TensorFold 49, vLLM 38, llama.cpp 33.
794 tok/s
Peak decode throughput at 64 requests, 4.3× TensorFold (184 at 16 requests, its stream limit).
150 tasks/h
Agentic tasks per hour with 16 agents on AgentPerf-Local, 3.1× vLLM (49). 168 at 32 agents.

Local agents keep extending long histories in the same memory that holds the model. Sharar decides what stays resident, what survives between turns, and what each accepted token costs.

Three co-designed techniques

Read fewer bytes, keep each agent's state, accept more per read

bytes read per token ↓

Model surgery

Editing a trained model's architecture to suit its hardware, so each token reads fewer bytes and the model takes less memory.

  • Experts and dense-layer decode copies as 3-bit FP8-codebook indices, run on FP8 tensor cores
  • Recurrent states quantized to INT8
  • A 2-bit output head shortlists candidates, then FP8 rescores them
work kept across turns ↑

Unified-memory management

Each agent's state survives across turns, so a long-running agent resumes instantly instead of recomputing its context.

  • SSD session cache: KV, recurrent and draft state, through a small fixed staging buffer
  • Engram offloading: large embedding tables served from the SSD
work per accepted token ↓

Adaptive speculation

More accepted tokens per weight read, by making each draft-verify round cheaper and longer where it pays.

  • Expert sharing across the tokens of a verify batch
  • Draft lengths adapted to acceptance rates; diffusion prefixes verified selectively
  • Optional acceptance of near-miss tokens

The exact profile serves the original model with exact verification; the fast profile, used for every result here, enables all optimizations. The tags in the figure above mark which steps change outputs.

Try it · adaptive speculation · expert sharing

A verify batch reads the union of every token's experts

In an MoE layer each token picks its own top-k experts, and verifying a batch of draft tokens must load every expert any of them chose. Sharar gives the batch a shared budget: each token's top choice is guaranteed, the remaining slots go to the experts with the most routing mass, and every token's second choice is taken from inside that set. Fewer distinct experts means fewer weight bytes per round.

Try it · adaptive speculation · adaptive drafting

Draft only as deep as acceptance pays for

Each extra draft token costs one more draft step and one more verification row. Sharar keeps a per-request estimate q of how often a drafted position is accepted, and picks the depth that maximizes expected tokens per unit of round time:

d* = argmax1≤d≤dmax (Σj=0..d qj) / (1 + c·(d − 1))

Move the sliders. High-acceptance text (code, repeated tool output) earns deep drafts; uncertain text earns shallow ones. Under exact verification this changes speed only, never the output.

Model surgery · draft head

A 2-bit draft head that still agrees with FP8

The draft model's vocabulary head is the largest matrix it reads every step. Sharar stores it in 2 bits and rescores the top-16 candidates in higher precision, which recovers agreement where it was lost: on uncertain tokens, where the naive 2-bit head picks a different token half the time. Only the drafter changes, so the target still decides every token.

Agreement with the FP8 head's token, binned by the FP8 head's entropy (bits). Overall agreement is in each legend entry.

Unified-memory management · SSD session cache

When agent sessions outgrow GPU memory, keep them on the SSD

192 AgentPerf-Local conversations replayed at once, so their combined context grows to about twice Sharar's GPU KV capacity. About 130 turns pass before a conversation returns, so without a second tier each one is evicted first and recomputes most of its context. The baselines keep the saved state of only 16 to 32 conversations and stay below 20% cache hits; Sharar without the SSD tier stays below about 35%.

Sharar writes each evicted conversation to the SSD and reads it back on its next turn. Its hit rate climbs to 80–98%, each turn recomputes about 600 tokens instead of 11,000, and median TTFT stays at a few seconds. The baselines' TTFT exceeds 100 s, up to 42× Sharar's.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next serving 192 agent conversations. Top: live session context, the tokens of all unfinished conversations; the dashed line is Sharar's GPU KV capacity (1.58 M tokens). Below: median TTFT (log scale) or the share of each prompt served from cache. 32 agents send turns back to back, thinking off, no tool time. Rolling medians; baseline runs were stopped after about 3.3k turns.

Results · four models, SPEED-Bench 16k and AgentPerf-Local

Faster for one user, and for many

Left, SPEED-Bench throughput on one DGX Spark as concurrency grows: each point is one concurrency level, per-user speed against total output throughput, so up and to the right is better. Sharar reaches higher throughput than every baseline at every concurrency level on all four models and scales to 64 requests; the baselines run out of memory for KV caches and recurrent states sooner. Right, agentic tasks per hour on AgentPerf-Local replay: at each system's best concurrency Sharar completes 1.5–3.4× more tasks per hour than the fastest baseline. Hover a point for its numbers.

The data of the paper's main results figure. SPEED-Bench with reasoning enabled, 16k prompts, log–log. Baselines run NVFP4 weights with their fastest drafter (DFlash2 for Qwen3.8-27B, the model's MTP head otherwise). Missing points are configurations a baseline could not run; TensorFold serves at most 16 streams.

Accuracy of the lossy optimizations

Within 3.6 points of the exact model

Three-bit weights, expert sharing, and relaxed verification can change outputs. Added one at a time on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, three-bit weights cost up to 2.3 points, expert sharing leaves every score unchanged, and relaxed verification costs up to 1.6 more. The full fast recipe stays within 3.6 points of the exact baseline on every benchmark.

Quick start

Serve a model on one Spark

Install uv, then:

# the repository opens with the paper
git clone https://github.com/abdelfattah-lab/sharar && cd sharar
uv sync
uv run sharar serve 27b          # Qwen3.8-27B on http://127.0.0.1:30001
uv run sharar serve flashnext    # Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (125B MoE)
uv run sharar launch claude      # point a coding agent at it

OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs, 262K context, one Spark or two over ConnectX. Add --exact for the model's own outputs.
